doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Taking over the estate, the LLC and Stolen Moments rights
summary: After the stepmother's death he and his brother formed an LLC, he sued a publisher, and he explains how his father sold the rights to Stolen Moments for 700 dollars.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well you’re fighting, what good is it going to do? You know what I mean? It just doesn’t make any sense at all. And then I’ve had a couple of — I had to learn the business of music on the fly because my stepmother basically controlled everything until she died. So © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

then my brother and I took it over, and I said well let’s put an LLC together. So we put an LLC and we structured it a couple of ways. We structured it first of all that the ownership would be 51-49. So I would be the 51 part and he would be the 49 part. He didn’t really like that but what that did for me was allow me to be able to do anything with anybody anywhere without having to contact him to get his permission, so I can make deals. And then we split the royalties 50-50. Well I ended up suing one company because they weren’t letting me exploit the music the way I wanted to. Of course that took two years and we got about 90 grand out of that one. But my dad learned the hard lesson with the music and I tell my students this all the time. He put out a piano book and it had eleven tunes in there, one of which was “Stolen Moments.” Of course musicians never know what their big hit’s going to be, and his goal in the early 50s was to be published and to be recorded. I mean that’s what you do. So for 700 dollars he basically kind of signed the rights away for that stuff, for 700 bucks, and “Stolen Moments” itself has brought in millions of dollars over that time span. So I had to sue these guys, and they paid us royalties before but you never know who’s honest and not. That’s the problem with the royalty business. Who’s really telling you the truth about this? So I have to live with them, and actually they got bought out, the company, Carlin America got bought out by a company called Round Hill Music which is owned by a bunch of investment bankers. So it’s kind of, when Carlin owned them it was really kind of music people. These guys now, you know they’re just in it for the money wherever they can get it. But they’ve been really good and this is the first time that I’ve worked with a company that I’ve never talked to anybody physically. Everything is by email. You know what I mean? And the other company I could call if I wanted to talk to the head of accounting, where’s my royalty check, I could call the guy and I knew who he was and that kind of stuff. But actually Carlin, they bought Carlin America up with 245 million dollars. Because they have stuff from James Brown, they had stuff from Elvis Presley, they had jazz guys, they had a lot of, you know ownership of tunes.
